To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we can partition a Web page (or a collection of pages) into semantically meaningful parts, (ii) we can identify the schema of a Web page (i.e., its template), (iii) we can identify a template for the content that changes in the page, and (iv) we can identify which parts of the content are semantically related to each other.

(1) the semantic partitioning of Web documents into their constituent components is useful for several Web applications, (2) the semantic partition of the Web is a challenging task due to the complexity of the underlying schemas, (3) the semantic partition can be achieved using machine learning techniques, (4) the resulting semantic partitions of the Web can be used to improve several Web applications.
In summary, our research is concerned with
extracting the schema of Web pages that contain machine-generated data (i.e., the data is generated by templates).
the problem of extracting a schema for a given Web page.
the problem of extracting the schema of a Web page.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the schema for a Web document is the set of all templates used in generating the document, together with all taxonomies that are used in the generation of the document.
the schema of the page includes the following: a taxonomy of items (which is fixed) and a template for each item.
the schema of a page is the structure that describes the layout and the content of the page.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how to use the schema for a Web document to improve Web search results.
it is the first work to provide a systematic study on semantic partitioning of machine-generated documents, where the schema is known.
we have developed a framework for the automatic extraction of schemas for a large class of Web pages.
The main takeaway from our work is that
by using the implicit schemas of Web pages, it becomes possible to partition the Web into a set of semantic classes of pages that are semantically similar.
by exploiting the implicit schema of a Web page, we are able to improve the performance of Web search engines.
if the schema is known then we can partition the page into several fragments and each fragment can be processed independently.
